opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, the hop languages were some of my favorite ones to design, because they target something linguists have argued about for a long time. Human languages don't seem to use counting rules. You don't find a grammar that says "put this agreement marker exactly four words after the verb." Grammatical rules tend to be structure-dependent: they care about hierarchy and constituents, not linear position.

So we made a controlled set of languages. Take English sentences, find the verbs, and replace the usual verb inflection with special marker tokens for singular or plural. In the control language, the marker sits right next to the verb, which is a natural, attested pattern. In the hop languages, the marker gets placed a fixed number of positions after the verb, four tokens in one version and four words in another. Everything else stays almost identical, so we can isolate the effect of a counting-based rule.

What I found interesting is that GPT-2 could learn these rules to some degree, but less efficiently than the natural control. When we looked at surprisal on the markers, the models did build up expectations about where the marker should go, so they're not blind to counting. But the learning was noticeably worse and slower than with the attested pattern.

That's a nuanced picture. There's been a claim that large language models can learn possible and impossible languages equally well, which would mean they tell us nothing about human language. The hop results push back on that. These models do have some inductive biases that line up with human language, and a counting rule is harder for them. It's not that the impossible language is unlearnable, but there's a real gradient of difficulty.

It also opens up good questions about what part of the architecture creates that bias. Is it the positional encodings? Attention? How tokenization interacts with the rule? Small, controlled manipulations like the hop languages let you ask those questions in a way you can't with natural data alone.

r001.rationale: The response says natural languages do not use rules placing an agreement marker exactly four words after a verb, but it describes only singular/plural marking and does not communicate the criterion’s tense-and-number marking target.

r002.rationale: The response reports that GPT-2 learned the hop rule less efficiently and more slowly than the adjacent-marker control, but describes only singular/plural markers, not tense-and-number markers as required.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the hop languages are probably my favorite part of the paper, because they're the ones where the result surprised me most. The setup is that we take English and insert a special token, a marker, before every verb. Then in the "no hop" version, the model just predicts the verb right after the marker, so it's basically English with an extra token. In the "token hop" version, the verb is shifted four tokens later, and in the "word hop" version, it's shifted four words later. So the model has to see the marker and then count forward to figure out where the verb inflection should land.

What's interesting is that these are, formally, pretty mild perturbations. None of this is unnatural in the sense of being random or structureless. There's a very simple, deterministic rule generating the data. If you believe that transformers are just general-purpose pattern learners, you'd expect them to pick up this rule with no trouble. But what we actually see is that perplexity gets steadily worse as you go from no hop to token hop to word hop. Counting a fixed number of tokens is harder for the model than you might think, and counting words is harder still, because word boundaries don't line up cleanly with tokens.

So I think the hop languages are a nice probe of a specific kind of inductive bias. GPT-2 doesn't have a built-in notion of "count four and then do something," and the attention mechanism isn't naturally suited to that kind of positional bookkeeping. Natural languages tend to avoid dependencies defined by counting. They prefer dependencies defined by structure, like agreement with a subject you can find hierarchically. The hop results suggest that the model's difficulty with counting dependencies actually lines up with the fact that human languages don't use them either. That's the broader point we were trying to make: the model isn't equally happy learning anything. There's a real sense in which it finds some impossible languages harder, and the hop languages are the clearest case where you can see that gradient emerge from a very small change to the input.

r001.rationale: The response says the word-hop setup places the verb inflection four words later and that natural languages avoid counting-defined dependencies.

r002.rationale: It reports steadily worse perplexity from no-hop to token-hop to word-hop, indicating worse prediction when the inflection is four words away than when it is adjacent.

astra-6.text:
What’s interesting about the hop languages is that they’re very close to English, but they introduce a rule that depends on counting words rather than on grammatical structure. You can imagine taking a grammatical marker and moving it a fixed number of words away from where it would normally appear. To predict where that marker goes, the model has to keep track of that count.

That gives us a way to ask a fairly specific question: Is a language model especially good at learning the kinds of rules we see in human languages, or can it just as readily learn this artificial counting rule? Because we’re perturbing English, we preserve a lot of the surrounding language and change one particular property. And counting might sound simple, but it isn’t necessarily simple for a model. That distinction—between what’s easy to describe and what’s easy to learn—is part of what makes these languages interesting.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s interesting about the hop languages is that they’re very close to English, but we introduce a rule that requires counting. For example, we can take a tense marker that would normally be attached to a verb and instead place it a fixed number of words away. To figure out where it belongs, you have to count words rather than follow the sentence’s syntactic structure.

That gives us a way to ask whether a language model finds those rules just as easy to learn as the kinds of rules we see in human languages. A transformer has access to positional information, so you might expect counting to be fairly easy for it. But being able to represent a rule doesn’t necessarily mean that it’s a rule the model readily learns. These languages help us probe that distinction.
